extracted.intended_audience: general readers and researchers looking for an encyclopedic summary of the book Three Cups of Tea and the related controversy
extracted.subtask_description: An encyclopedic entry summarizing the memoir Three Cups of Tea, its publication history, claims about humanitarian work, ensuing criticisms and investigations, legal outcomes, and reception. Useful for readers seeking an overview of the book and controversies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factual accuracy of events recounted
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether events described in the memoir actually occurred (e.g., Mortenson getting lost after K2, stumbling into Korphe, promising to build a school; capture by the Taliban).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allegations include that “some of the events recounted in Three Cups of Tea ... did not take place,” and specific incidents (K2 descent, capture) are disputed by reporters and local sources; corroboration by independent sources and consistency of timelines are relevant. Anti-pattern: relying solely on a single, uncorroborated personal narrative for key factual claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Journalistic objectivity and authorship attribution
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the reporting and authorship behind the book were objective and properly credited (Relin's role and potential bias).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article notes Relin admitted his desire to see Mortenson's project succeed likely influenced his objectivity and that Relin later said Mortenson should not have been named a co-author. Evaluate whether the journalist's relationship with the subject affected fact-checking, transparency about roles, and authorship credit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verification and corroboration of claims
rubrics_metrics.description: The degree to which claims (about schools built, incidents, timelines) are independently verifiable and supported by documentation or third-party reporting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The piece cites journalists (e.g., Jon Krakauer), television investigations (60 Minutes), and later CAI project lists; examples of unverifiable or contradicted claims are given. Good practice: cite contemporaneous records, local testimony, and multiple independent sources; anti-pattern: accepting anecdote without corroboration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Charitable financial stewardship and use of funds
rubrics_metrics.description: How the Central Asia Institute (CAI) used donated funds and whether spending aligned with charitable mission (building/supporting schools).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criticism includes that only 41 percent of money raised in 2009 went to build schools and allegations that Mortenson misspent funds; the Montana inquiry found misspending of over $6 million and resulted in Mortenson repaying $1 million. Metrics: percent of donations spent on program services vs. fundraising/administration, existence of misspent funds, and outcomes tied to spending.

rubrics_metrics.name: Overhead, advertising, and travel spending compared to peers
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether spending on advertising, authors' promotion, and travel (including private jets) was excessive relative to comparable charitable institutions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 60 Minutes alleged CAI’s amount spent on advertising Mortenson's books and paying travel expenses was excessive relative to comparable charities. Evaluate via benchmarking overhead ratios and specific expenditures on promotion vs. program delivery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Program impact, sustainability, and on-the-ground use
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether claimed schools were actually built, maintained, and used for education rather than abandoned or repurposed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allegations: some schools 'either have not been built, have been built and abandoned, are used for other purposes such as grain storage, or have not been supported by CAI after they were built.' Impact assessment should examine site visits, local testimony, ongoing support, and current usage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency, record-keeping, and governance
rubrics_metrics.description: Quality of CAI’s record-keeping, internal controls, board oversight, and response to inquiries about 'excess benefits' or conflicts of interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montana AG said Mortenson's 'disregard for and attitude about basic record-keeping and accounting' had significant effects; CAI retained counsel to investigate 'excess benefits.' Evaluate whether the charity maintained adequate records, independent oversight, and transparent reporting to donors and regulators.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal and investigatory outcomes and accountability
rubrics_metrics.description: Results of official investigations, lawsuits, and settlements relating to the book and the charity (e.g., Montana attorney general inquiry, repayment, dismissed lawsuits, appeals).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page documents a Montana investigation (resulting in $1 million repayment but no criminality found), dismissed class-action suits, and appellate decisions; use these outcomes to judge legal accountability and corrective actions taken.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reception, recognition, and public influence
rubrics_metrics.description: Measures of the book’s public reception such as bestseller status, awards, and influence on public discourse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Three Cups of Tea 'remained on the New York Times nonfiction bestseller's list for four years' and received multiple awards (Kiriyama Prize, Time Magazine Asia Book of the Year, etc.). Reception can be used to assess cultural impact but should be weighed separately from factual and governance assessments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethical considerations of co-authorship and narrator perspective
rubrics_metrics.description: Ethical questions about crediting a co-author when the narrative perspective and reporting may not support equal authorship.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article notes the book is 'written from Relin's perspective as a journalist interviewing and observing Mortenson' and that Relin later said Mortenson should not have been named a co-author. Relevant evaluation: transparency about who produced the reporting, how narrative voice was assigned, and whether byline reflects contributions.
